passage:
Aditi walked into the Class 9 lab just as Ishita's table burst out laughing. Aditi's stomach dropped. Her hair? The stain on her sleeve? She slid onto the far stool and kept her eyes on the burner.
At lunch she had messaged Ishita, 'partners for the project?' The two ticks had turned blue at 1:10. It was now 2:40. No reply.
So that's it, Aditi thought. They've decided.
When Ishita leaned over and whispered, 'Did you see Harshit's goggles? They're on upside down,' Aditi only shrugged and said, 'I'm working with Neel.'
Ishita blinked. 'Oh. Okay.' She turned back to her table.
Aditi stared at the flame, hands cold, sure now that she had been right all along.

qa.q: At what time did the ticks on Aditi's message turn blue?
qa.a: The two ticks turned blue at 1:10.

qa.q: What was Aditi afraid the laughter meant?
qa.a: She feared the table was laughing at her hair or the stain on her sleeve, and took the missing reply to mean they had decided to drop her.

qa.q: What could Aditi try at this stage to test her fear?
qa.a: She could treat her first reading as a guess, laugh at the goggles with Ishita and simply ask about the project, since the joke showed the laughter wasn't about her.

qa.q: How might Ishita experience Aditi's shrug and 'I'm working with Neel'?
qa.a: Ishita reached out with a joke and got a cold reply, so she may feel brushed off and conclude Aditi doesn't want her as a partner 😔

grounding: It shows a lonely teenager reading a laugh and a slow reply as dislike, then acting guarded in a way that pushes her friend away.

passage:
Dear Bidisha Apu,
You said to write when things feel heavy, so here I am.
School has been strange since you left. On Monday I posted in the class group asking if anyone had the chemistry notes. Forty minutes, nothing. Then Rumana replied 'check the drive' with no emoji. Not even a smiley. I read that about ten times.
At lunch, Tasnim said something and everyone laughed just as I sat down. I'm almost sure it was about me. So now I eat quickly and go to the library, and when people talk to me I answer in one word, and they've mostly stopped talking to me. Which proves it, doesn't it?
Or does it? I can't tell anymore.
Write back soon 🥺
Nazia

qa.q: What did Rumana reply after forty minutes?
qa.a: Rumana replied 'check the drive' with no emoji.

qa.q: Why did Nazia read Rumana's reply about ten times?
qa.a: Nazia was searching it for signs of dislike, because a lonely, worried mind was treating a missing smiley as a threat.

qa.q: What could help Nazia step out of this loop?
qa.a: Nazia could list other reasons for the slow reply and the laugh, and try one warmer answer at lunch to see what actually happens 🙂

qa.q: How might the classmates see Nazia's one-word answers?
qa.a: They might think Nazia wants to be left alone, so they talk less, which then feels like proof of the rejection Nazia feared.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a late reply and a laugh as dislike, becoming guarded and quiet in a way that seems to confirm the fear.

passage:
Noor sent Mehak a long message at 7 p.m. about the science project. By 9 there was no reply, though the ticks showed it had been read. Noor lay on her bed in their Delhi flat and replayed the day. Mehak had laughed at lunch when Noor spilled her juice. Not a mean laugh, maybe. But maybe.
By 10 Noor had decided: Mehak was tired of her. Everyone probably was.
Next morning in class Mehak waved. "Sorry, my phone died after I read it, and then Mummy made me do the dishes." Noor heard only the sorry and nodded stiffly. "It's fine. I'll do the project myself."
Mehak's smile faded. "Oh. Okay."
Noor went back to her desk, stomach tight. See, she thought. She doesn't even care. She didn't notice that it was her own cold voice that had closed the door.

qa.q: Why did Mehak say she didn't reply?
qa.a: Her phone died after she read it, and then Mummy made her do the dishes.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling by 10 p.m.?
qa.a: Noor felt lonely and rejected, reading the late reply and the lunch laugh as proof Mehak was tired of her.

qa.q: What could Noor try next time a reply is late?
qa.a: Remind herself of other reasons, like a dead phone, and ask Mehak warmly instead of pulling away.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel when Noor says she'll do the project herself?
qa.a: Mehak likely feels confused and hurt, pushed away after a genuine apology.

grounding: A lonely teen reads a late reply and a laugh as dislike, turns guarded, and her coldness makes the rejection she feared more likely.

passage:
"Why didn't you save me a seat on the bus?" Chinmay asked, dropping his bag.
"I did! Then Kunal sat there before I could say anything."
"Right."
"What's 'right' supposed to mean?"
"Nothing. You were all laughing at the back when I got on."
"At the video Kunal was showing. The goat one."
"Sure. The goat."
"Chinmay, what's going on? You've been weird for days."
"You didn't reply to my message on Saturday either."
"I was at my cousin's wedding! I replied on Sunday."
"Eleven hours later."
Mridul stared. "You counted?"
Chinmay looked at the floor. He had counted. He had also decided, somewhere between the bus steps and the back seat, that they all found him boring. "Forget it," he muttered.
"I'm not going to forget it. Sit with me at lunch. Please."

qa.q: Why didn't Mridul reply on Saturday?
qa.a: Mridul was at a cousin's wedding.

qa.q: What does Chinmay counting the hours reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: He feels lonely and anxious, reading small delays and laughter as proof that his friends find him boring.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do instead of saying 'Forget it'?
qa.a: Accept Mridul's lunch invitation and say honestly that he felt left out on the bus.

qa.q: What is this conversation like for Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul feels confused and a bit hurt at being accused, but cares enough to insist on lunch.

grounding: A lonely teen takes a lost seat, a laugh and a slow reply as signs of dislike, and his guardedness strains the friendship.

passage:
Last term I was sure Bidisha had started to dislike me. It began with small things. She replied to my messages hours late. In the canteen she whispered something to Tashi and they both laughed, and my face burned. I decided the laugh was about me.
So I got guarded. I stopped sitting with them. When Bidisha asked if I wanted to share notes, I said, "I'm fine," in a voice even I could hear was cold. She looked hurt and stopped asking. That felt like proof.
It wasn't. Months later Bidisha told me she'd been laughing at a teacher's spelling mistake on the board, and that her late replies were because her grandmother was in hospital. She thought I was the one who had gone off her.
I'm Vinita, and I still think about how loneliness had me reading every signal upside down.

qa.q: Why were Bidisha's replies late?
qa.a: Her grandmother was in hospital.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when Bidisha and Tashi laughed in the canteen?
qa.a: Vinita felt embarrassed and rejected, face burning, sure the laugh was mockery.

qa.q: What could Vinita have done when the laugh stung?
qa.a: Asked Bidisha lightly what was funny, or checked in about the late replies, instead of turning cold.

qa.q: How did Bidisha experience Vinita's coldness?
qa.a: Bidisha felt hurt and confused, believing Vinita was the one who had gone off her.

grounding: A teen looks back on how loneliness made her read late replies and a laugh as rejection, and her guardedness confirmed the fear.

passage:
Note from the drama club teacher, Tuesday rehearsal
Trisha has been with the club since August and is usually quiet but prepared. Today, during the scene break, Hemant laughed at something on his phone just as Trisha finished her lines. She went red, stepped back and did not speak again for the rest of the rehearsal. When the group chat went silent for an hour after she posted the new costume list, she messaged me: "I think everyone finds me annoying." In the next scene her voice was so low the others kept asking her to repeat, which made her more flustered.
What I did next: I checked with Hemant privately; he had been laughing at a video from his cousin and hadn't noticed Trisha at all. After rehearsal I sat with Trisha for a few minutes and asked what other explanations there might be for the laugh and the quiet chat. I have also paired her with Hemant for Thursday's prop work.

qa.q: What did Trisha post before the group chat went silent for an hour?
qa.a: She posted the new costume list.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling after Hemant laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and afraid, taking the laugh as a sign that everyone found her annoying.

qa.q: What turning point did the teacher offer, and why is it useful?
qa.a: The teacher helped Trisha look for other explanations for the laugh and the quiet chat, and paired her with Hemant so she can test her fear against real contact.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel if he learns Trisha thought he was laughing at her?
qa.a: Hemant would probably be surprised and a little sorry, since he was only watching his cousin's video and hadn't noticed her.

grounding: Shows a lonely teenager reading a laugh and a quiet chat as dislike, becoming more guarded and awkward in a way that feeds the fear.
